audit.action: a better source should be cited for the same classification
audit.reasoning: Coding 'tonal' (three level tones H/M/L plus contours; no word-stress rule; 'accent d'intensité' only as the donor-language stress of French loans reinterpreted as a falling tone) rests on the right work — Nougayrol 1979, the sole reference grammar and best of only three Glottolog descriptive refs, with no later phonology/prosody study found by web search. The deciding quote fragments are verbatim in the snippet files we hold, and an independent open source downloaded now (Hyman & Leben 2017 p.196, citing Nougayrol 1979:161) confirms the H/M/L tonal contrast. The only weakness is access: the primary is held as Google Books snippets, print-only otherwise. Nothing suggests the classification would change. Action: add Hyman & Leben 2017 p.196 as a corroborating page-cited source now; a library read of Nougayrol 1979 ch. 1 would lift the grade from 'snippet' to full-page.

sources.quote: 'A similar situation arises in Day [Adamawa; Chad] in the marking of aspect (Nougayrol 1979:161). Although the language contrasts surface H, M, and L we again recognize inputs /H/ and /L/ ...' with yúú/yūū/yùù aspect alternations (completive H- prefix, incompletive L- prefix; H+L and L+H both surface as M). No mention of stress/accent in Day.
